lesson.title: When More Isn't Faster: Zero-Order Reactions
lesson.summary: In a zero-order reaction the rate is constant and completely independent of reactant concentration, typically because something other than the reactant, like a saturated catalyst surface, is what actually limits how fast the reaction can proceed.
lesson.body:
A zero-order reaction is one where the reaction order with respect to a given reactant is 0. Plugging that into the rate law gives rate = k[A]^0. Since any nonzero number raised to the power 0 equals 1, this simplifies to rate = k. In other words, the rate is simply equal to the rate constant, a fixed number, no matter what [A] happens to be at any given moment. This is genuinely counterintuitive the first time you see it: common sense says more reactant should mean a faster reaction, but zero order kinetics says otherwise, at least with respect to that particular species.

Physically, zero order behavior shows up when something other than reactant concentration is the true bottleneck on reaction speed. A classic scenario is a reaction catalyzed by a solid surface or an enzyme that has become saturated, every available active site on the catalyst is already occupied and working as fast as it can, so piling on more reactant molecules in solution just means more molecules waiting in line, it does not speed up the processing rate of the catalyst itself. The catalyst, not the concentration of A, is what sets the pace.

Here is a worked numeric illustration. Suppose a heterogeneous catalytic decomposition has been experimentally determined to be zero order, with rate constant k = 0.0050 M/s. At [A] = 0.80 M, the rate is rate = k[A]^0 = 0.0050 M/s x (0.80)^0 = 0.0050 M/s x 1 = 0.0050 M/s. Now let the reaction proceed until [A] has fallen to 0.40 M, half its original value. The rate is rate = k[A]^0 = 0.0050 M/s x (0.40)^0 = 0.0050 M/s x 1 = 0.0050 M/s, exactly the same number. Cutting the concentration in half changed the rate not at all, which is the defining signature of zero order kinetics.

One caveat is essential to keep in mind: this constant rate cannot continue forever. It only holds while some reactant A remains available to feed the catalyst or process at all. Once A is entirely consumed, the rate has nowhere to go but down to zero, since a reaction obviously cannot continue once its reactant is gone. That transition, and exactly how concentration falls over time under zero order kinetics, is worked out precisely in the zero-order integrated rate law chapter later in this unit.
